articles.title: Ryan Crowley: Airman's rugby career has taken off at Leicester Tigers
articles.summary: BBC Sport meets Ryan Crowley, the airman whose rugby career has taken off at Prem giants Leicester Tigers.
articles.body:
Corporal Ryan Crowley has spent a decade helping get aircraft off the ground.

It has taken just as long for the winger to finally get his professional rugby union career to take off.

It was only a year ago that Crowley was plucked from his role as an avionics engineer with the Royal Air Force and recruited by Leicester Tigers.

The 28-year-old Welshman was handed a deal with the giants of the game, the 11-time Prem champions - when he didn't even know one was up for grabs.

"I thought I got sent up to Tigers to go and get experience and do a pre-season with a pro team," he told BBC Sport.

The military man had simply followed orders.

Chinnor, the second division side he was playing for, asked him to join Geoff Parling's Tigers for the early weeks of their Prem Rugby Cup campaign last season.

"After a couple of weeks Geoff said, 'you've been successful in your trial', and I was like, 'what trial?'," Crowley added.

"The silver lining to not knowing it was a trial is I had no pressure on me; I just came up and I was just trying to learn as much as I could.

"I didn't have any expectations of having to come out the end of it with something, but luckily I did."

Winger Crowley joins Tigers after successful trial

Listen to the Tigers Rugby Show on BBC Radio Leicester

Crowley saw out the season with Tigers, playing seven Prem Rugby Cup games, and was handed a new one-year deal to remain with the club this term.

It was after that contract extension that Crowley was able to tell Parling what it meant to him to be a full-time professional after years of dedication to the British Armed Forces.

Even now Crowley remains part of the RAF.

But through its elite athlete scheme, he has been allowed to step back from his role to pursue his playing career with Tigers.

"When Geoff told me he wanted me to stay, I said to him that for a very young Ryan Crowley this was a dream come true," the winger explained.

"I did think my ship had sailed - but I kept training and kept going."

Crowley grew up playing for St Peter's in Cardiff and had a spell with Welsh Premiership side Pontypridd before enlisting to become an airman when he was still a teenager.

At that point, rugby became something he did alongside his basic training at RAF Halton in Buckinghamshire and his studies in avionics, which took him to RAF Cosford in Shropshire.

For much of the next 10 years his focus was on carrying out maintenance and repairs on the sophisticated electronics on military aircraft - which has included Boeing C-17 Globemaster military transporters worth more than £250m.

And yet, his career in the military was never an excuse to give up on making it as a rugby player.

The RAF has played a significant role in that, with Crowley representing them in inter-services matches, while he has also played on the global stage for the UK Armed Forces.

During the three years he spent becoming a fully qualified aircraft engineer he was playing club rugby in the lower leagues, but after that he leaped up the divisions when signed by second-tier side London Scottish in 2020.

It had appeared to be a career breakthrough.

But funding cuts by English rugby's governing body, the Rugby Football Union (RFU), that same year, as well as the financial fallout of the Covid-19 pandemic, forced the club to shift from being a full-time professional outfit to a part-time, semi-professional side by the time Crowley joined them.

"I'd often say to my family that I felt like I had the worst luck in rugby," Crowley said.

"I was always close to something happening, like with what happened at London Scottish, then I'd miss out. I've had injuries at different times that have also stopped me from taking opportunities.

"But I've not given up and have always kept knocking on the door. I didn't really see any other choice - rugby is my life and I kept playing. I've been obsessed with rugby since I was old enough to pick a ball up and throw it around.

"And it's finally worked out for me and I've got to where I want to be."

'I'm competing against myself, learning from them'

At Tigers he has taken his place among a stable of international wingers, including Wales' Gabriel Hamer-Webb and England pair Adam Radwan and Ollie Hassell-Collins.

Crowley has so far featured 10 times for Tigers, with all those appearances coming in the Prem Cup.

And while he was named in a matchday squad for a European Champions Cup match last season, he never made it off the bench.

"It's been challenging, but I wouldn't say challenging in a negative way," Crowley said.

"Having the likes of Radas, Hass and Gabe in front of me, I never really came into this thinking I'm competing against them. And while I actually am, I'm competing against myself to see how far I can get.

"I'm learning from them because they've been in the system and this environment for so long.

"There is a lot of healthy competition in the team but we are all extremely close - with lots of group chats and good banter as we wind each other up.

"When we step on to that pitch we do drive each other, the switch gets flicked and we are on it, but as soon as we are off it we are back to the jokes."

And how does being a corporal in the RAF, who has turned into a Tigers winger, fare when it comes to the mickey-taking of team-mates?

It turns out that while he has managed to fly under the radar by avoiding any military-style nicknames, his team-mates have instead chosen to lean into his 5ft 7in (1.7m) stature instead.

"I do get the banter about my height, but I'm an easy target for that one," he said.

"I just kind of live it and wear it as a badge to be fair because being probably one of the smallest people in the Prem, to be at this level, I think, is an achievement."

Post-match round-ups and analysis on all things Tigers

articles.title: Rassie Erasmus: South Africa coach invites fans to watch-along of Springboks clash vs Ireland following six-match ban
articles.summary: Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus was handed a six-match suspension for comments he made about referees following South Africa's Nations Championship defeat by France; South Africa Rugby have requested a full hearing into his ban
articles.body:
Erasmus had questioned whether there were double standards in the officiating of South Africa's 21-19 defeat to France during a press conference earlier in the week, prompting an investigation from World Rugby , who later said that the coach had "disrespected the authority of the officials".

He will now be unable to have any match-day involvement in his side's Nations Championship match against Ireland on Saturday, or their Nations Championship Finals match, commencing the following week.

South Africa have requested a full hearing in response to the sanction and on Wednesday, Erasmus broke his silence, inviting members of the public to join him to watch Saturday's game via a live stream.

"Can sit and moan or make the best of it," the Springboks coach wrote in a post on X.

"I'll be watching the match at the hotel. Not keen to watch [it] on my own.

"So, let's give it a go and hope I get the 'tech' sorted = TV on, My Laptop camera on, and you're welcome to join me.

"Sign up here (adults 18+): . This is personal, not official."

On his streaming website, Erasmus has embedded a video of a flying South Africa flag, with a link to sign up to watch.

The 54-year-old, who guided South Africa to back-to-back Rugby World Cups in 2019 and 2023, provided some more details on the webpage about how the live stream would work.

"We each watch on our own TV, and I'll be on camera so you can see me watch it too. Send me a message and I'll read some out."

A disclaimer on the page read: "This is me personally, Rassie. It is not an official team or Springbok channel."

It is unclear when Erasmus will be able to return to coach South Africa, but he is expected to be available for the 2027 Rugby World Cup.

On Tuesday, World Rugby confirmed an independent panel had reviewed the comments made by Erasmus under World Rugby's Match Official Abuse Sanction Process, a framework that was introduced in July.

"The panel determined that the comments suggest that match officials acted with bias/prejudice or deliberately influenced the outcome of a match, and when the conduct is considered as a whole a reasonable person would conclude that the conduct constituted an unacceptable attack on the credibility and competence of the match officials," the governing body said in a statement.

"In respect to the sanction, the panel determined that the conduct clearly amounts to disrespecting the authority of the match officials by impugning their integrity."

Erasmus: Manipulation of the game or the result?

On Monday, Erasmus claimed France should have been given three yellow cards for illegal tackles as he leapt into a rant criticising referees.

"Let's say 11 of those were at least a penalty and three I thought were at least three yellow cards. And not one was sanctioned and not one was shown out or cited," Erasmus said.

"I'll send you the playlist, but I'll get into trouble… So I can't send the playlist to anybody and we can only send five clips to World Rugby. So we'll probably query it, but the answer will probably be: 'Yes, it was a mistake; it should have been penalised'.

"On numerous times we mentioned to the referee 'we think there's a knee-drop tackle'. I'm saying to you, my feeling is that knee-drop tackles is out. They happened 17 times in our game. Not one was penalised.

"And if the TMO didn't see it, then maybe technology must be better. If he saw it and ignored it, what does that boil down to? Manipulation of the game or the result? Or players getting injured?

"So, all I'm asking is don't take the TMOs out and discourage them from getting involved. Then the wrong team will win and players will get injured. That's all I'm saying."

World Rugby has since received backlash on social media in the wake of Erasmus' ban, and South Africa Rugby has condemned the abuse.

"SA Rugby unequivocally condemns any form of intimidation, threats or personal attacks. Such behaviour has no place in rugby and is entirely contrary to the values upon which our game is founded."

images.caption: Image: Erasmus broke his silence on X regarding his six-game ban
Image: World Rugby suspended the coach after he criticised the officiating of his side's defeat against France
Image: Rassie Erasmus has been handed a six-game ban for comments he made following his side's defeat to France last Friday

articles.title: England v New Zealand: Jack van Poortvliet on 2022 All Blacks nightmare
articles.summary: Jack van Poortvliet was picked off and subbed off when he last met the All Blacks. Four years on, he says the experience made him a better player.
articles.body:
A mocking pat on the back from Codie Taylor. A close-up of his own face on the Twickenham big screen. A painful inquest under the sticks.

Jack van Poortvliet's first meeting with New Zealand was only four minutes old when it curdled sour.

In November 2022 Van Poortvliet, then 21, was winning only his sixth cap.

Sharing the scrum-half duties with England veterans Ben Youngs and Richard Wigglesworth, he had been a key part in Leicester's run to the Premiership title the previous season. Van Poortvliet was touted as the next big thing at Test level too.

But, off an early England line-out, Van Poortvliet, focused on Owen Farrell's hands, failed to spot Dalton Papali'i flying up out of the line.

The All Black flanker picked off the interception and cantered in for the game's opening try.

Van Poortvliet's afternoon ended after 54 minutes. With England trailing 22-6, his final act was a knock-on after being harried by Brodie Retallick at the back of a breakdown. His mistake squandered a prime attacking position.

Eddie Jones had seen enough, withdrawing Van Poortvliet and bringing on Ben Youngs.

England would go on to draw the game 25-25 after a remarkable late rally. But there was no rallying Van Poortvliet.

"I remember just being pretty disappointed," he told BBC Sport.

"It was the first time I had felt what it was like to play for my country and not deliver how I wanted to.

"I care a lot about how I play and how I perform. At that time, I wasn't very good at letting stuff go or managing how I was when things went against me. I remember being pretty down."

It was a difficult time for England as a whole.

Van Poortvliet retained his place, but a 27-13 defeat by South Africa the following weekend signalled the end of Jones' England reign. An eyesore of a Six Nations campaign, including a record 53-10 home defeat by France, followed a few months later.

Van Poortvliet, who had read online praise on his rise to Test level, was now exposed to keyboard criticism.

When he suffered a serious ankle injury in a warm-up Test against Wales before the 2023 World Cup, he received posts celebrating his absence from the tournament.

But Van Poortvliet says his performance against New Zealand, and the criticism that followed, was the start of learning to leave mistakes in the past.

"It was probably a good thing that I had that [performance against New Zealand] so early on," he said.

"I probably stopped taking myself so seriously and gained the ability to let go [of past mistakes] in game.

"You're not defined by one moment in a game. If there's a couple of errors, mistakes happen. You're never going to play the perfect game. It was one of those big lessons for me."

Alex Mitchell leapt to the top of England's scrum-half pecking order at France 2023.

But Mitchell's injuries, combined with Van Poortvliet's smart form for table-topping Leicester, mean the Tigers man is back in possession of England's number nine shirt.

Van Poortvliet made only his third England start since 2023 in July's Nations Championship opener against South Africa and has been in place ever since.

Presuming he retains his spot, Saturday will be his first encounter with New Zealand since his 2022 horror show.

Listen to match commentary on BBC Radio 5 Extra, BBC Sounds, BBC Sport website and through your smart speaker

The All Blacks are recovering from their own, more recent, disappointment.

Coach Dave Rennie said his players "let their country down" in a shock defeat by Wales last weekend.

Van Poortvliet expects them to react with the level-headedness he himself has learned.

"They had a disappointing result last week, which happens. We've had plenty in the past," he said.

"Most good teams don't have two poor performances in a row and good teams normally respond well.

"We're excited to take on the best version of New Zealand."

After Cortez Ratima deputised in defeat by Wales, Van Poortvliet is likely to be up against Cam Roigard, whose relatively tall stature and running game are a similar match to his own.

But, four years on and with the World Cup looming once more, England are also seeing the best version of Van Poortvliet again.

images.caption: Image caption, Jack van Poortvliet, who made a try-scoring debut against Australia in 2022, has won 29 Test caps
Image caption, Scrum-half Aaron Smith told Van Poortvliet after New Zealand's 2022 win that the All Blacks had targetted stealing interceptions off his pass

articles.title: PWR: RFU wants to 'protect Red Roses' with reduction in international players
articles.summary: The RFU wants PWR to protect the interests of England's Red Roses, which could see a reduction in the number of international players in the league.
articles.body:
World rugby has endured a few shocks and upsets in 2026 - and England's women losing back-to-back Test matches to Canada was among the biggest.

But with 25 Canadians plying their trade on English soil in Premiership Women's Rugby (PWR) last season, their success on the international stage comes at a time when PWR has been in discussions with the Rugby Football Union (RFU) to review the numbers of overseas players in the league.

"We are keen to attract star talent into PWR to continue to make it the best league in the world," said RFU chief executive Bill Sweeney.

"But we've also got to protect England Red Roses' interests as well."

Changes have been planned for the 2027-28 PWR season around injury dispensation for foreign players, with the removal of club injury credit which helps to cover the cost of replacing an injured player.

Only players who sustain an injury while on international duty for one of England's representative teams will be eligible.

However, discussions have gone further around the numbers of English Qualified Players (EQP) required in matchday squads.

Speaking to BBC Sport, Sweeney said: "We're talking about it. Currently, there's 13 EQP in PWR. It's 15 in the [men's] Prem.

"We're always concerned about the amount of game time that's occurring for under-23 players coming through the system. Are they getting enough game time?

"We're having conversations with PWR in terms of how we can maximise that, so it is a live topic."

No panic for England but Mitchell issues PWR warning

Bristol will 'bring out' best version of Kildunne

England had been on a 41-match unbeaten streak - dating back almost four years - before twice losing to Canada in the WXV Global Series last month.

It prompted a warning from head coach John Mitchell that too many overseas players in the PWR could be detrimental for future Red Roses sides.

The league has increasingly attracted the best global talent. In recent years, a majority of Scotland and Wales players have played in PWR and since the 2025 World Cup, more players have joined from New Zealand.

The highest-profile arrival last season was Black Ferns captain Ruahei Demant linking up with Bristol, while Ruby Tui has joined Trailfinders Women for the new campaign.

And while many neutrals believe Canada's growing success is good for the women's game, Sweeney says England must keep "raising the bar".

"It doesn't feel it's good for the game for us, we never want to lose - but it had to come at some stage," he said.

"Seeing the growth in the Canadian team, largely due to where they play in PWR - it's encouraging that the standards are rising.

"We're conscious that unions like Ireland are investing much more heavily now into the women's game as well, so it is good for the game.

"From our perspective, we just want to keep raising the bar and challenging people to catch us and challenge us."

IRFU await news of 'massive opportunity' to join PWR

Fewer international stars would 'diminish quality of PWR'

Canada and Saracens scrum-half Olivia Apps was named PWR player of the season when her club lifted the 2025-26 trophy.

She says exposure to the PWR has massively benefited Canadian rugby.

"It's the best women's league right now to play in and the best quality competition," she told BBC Sport.

"We don't have a league back home, so to be able to come from the universities and play with and against the best players in the world is going to make us better for sure."

Asked if she was worried Canadian players would not get as much game time in the future, Apps said: "I would hope not. I think that would diminish the quality of the PWR.

"Internationals make this league what it is, and credit to the English players, but the internationals really do contribute in a great way.

"Any coach or team that has a Canadian on their side loves to have that Canadian because they work hard, they bring the physicality, the athleticism and a great style of rugby."

Reducing foreign imports would allow young English talent more PWR game time, but the move does not come without concerns.

"The league itself is to create Red Roses and to create English players for the future. If we are going to bring non-EQP players into the league, then they have to add to the league, so they have to be of a world-class standard," said Loughborough Lightning head coach Nathan Smith.

But Smith does envisage a problem if the league changes before investing in the pathways.

"There's a pinch point at the start of next season where we'll have Lions, England camp and a Premiership Cup. My simple question is, are there enough players to fulfil all three?" he said.

"England Under-20s and Under-18s aren't performing on the world stage, therefore what can we do to support that? We need a level of competition that sits below the PWR that fulfils their needs for development."

A PWR spokesperson said: "There is no difference of opinion between us and the RFU on this and developing the next generation of Red Roses is a specific, stated objective of the PWR.

"We will continue to work collaboratively with the RFU on EQP and any other matter which is important to the future of women's rugby in this country."

The new PWR season starts on Friday as Loughborough Lightning host Trailfinders.

For now, overseas stars will remain a key part of the league's success, but how many are allowed to feature in the future may define its next chapter.

images.caption: Image caption, (Left to right) Sophie de Goede, Hope Rogers, Ruby Tui and Olivia Apps are among PWR's foreign players

articles.title: Ireland v South Africa: Rassie Erasmus ban 'not dominating the coffee room' - Timoney
articles.summary: Ireland back row Nick Timoney says players are "not living under a rock" but any talk of Rassie Erasmus' six-game ban is not dominating their conversations.
articles.body:
Ireland back row Nick Timoney says players are "not living under a rock" but any talk of Rassie Erasmus' six-game ban is not dominating their conversations.

South Africa will face Ireland on Saturday in Dublin without their head coach after Erasmus was sanctioned for a third time by World Rugby.

Speaking at a news conference in Dublin on Monday, Erasmus questioned what he perceived as double standards in officiating to the point where he asked: "Is that not match-fixing?"

"You'd be amazed at how little rugby players are in the online rugby space," Timoney said when asked about the 54-year-old's comments.

"You tend to, for whatever reason, avoid it as best you can. Just more so you don't see the player ratings after a bad loss, or whatever it is.

"Obviously, I'm sure we're not living under a rock here but it's certainly not dominating the coffee room, you could say."

Before his match-fixing comments, Erasmus predicted that Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast would not be banned for a hip-drop tackle against Fiji because of a "technicality".

On Wednesday, World Rugby confirmed the 23-year-old would be free to face the back-to-back world champions on Saturday [16:40 GMT].

"It's kind of what we expected but I'm delighted for Sam and the rest of us," added Timoney.

"It's good it's over with nice and early in the week so we can focus on the game."

Divide and conquer - now maverick Erasmus plans online watchalong

'Is that not match-fixing?' - Erasmus questions officiating

Andy Farrell will name his side to face the Springboks on Thursday at 14:00 GMT.

Timoney said it was "an enormous game" as Ireland look to finish the Nations Championship with a third win in a row.

After wins over Australia and Japan were followed by a loss to New Zealand, Farrell's side have started November's window with victories over Argentina and Fiji.

Both Ireland and South Africa, who lost to France in their last match, have the opportunity to finish top of their respective northern and southern hemisphere groups.

When asked if Ireland were still hurting from their defeat by the Springboks in Dublin last year - when the visitors ran out 24-13 winners - Timoney looked at the bigger picture.

"I think we're hurting from not quite being where we want to be," he added.

"We obviously want to be the best team in the world like everyone else does. Being 100% honest, we're probably not quite there yet even though we have been in the past.

"There's no shying away from the fact they beat us at home last year. There's all sorts of points we want to prove but largely to ourselves."

Timoney, who has started Ireland's last 10 Tests, said the versatility of Saturday's opponents is one of their major strengths.

"They've not become double world champions by having one easy trick to beating them.

"We've just got to be excellent in all areas and it's going to take a massive effort certainly."

He added that Ireland are "pretty confident with our plan going in" and they have been building towards the final match in Dublin, before the Nations Championships' finals weekend in London.

"We're really looking forward to it and we've been building towards it. The last 12-24 months haven't been 100% what we've wanted the whole time.

"We feel like we're building nicely. The coaching, the players within the group, they're all world class. We can only be going in the right direction."

images.caption: Image caption, South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus was banned for six matches by World Rugby

articles.title: Wales v Australia: Steve Tandy makes four changes to side that beat All Blacks
articles.summary: Wales make four changes to their starting line-up that beat the All Blacks for the Nations Championship meeting with Australia.
articles.body:
Wales have made four changes to the side that made history against New Zealand for the Nations Championship fixture against Australia.

Head coach Steve Tandy has tinkered with the starting line-up that beat the All Blacks for the first time in 73 years at Principality Stadium.

Wales go with the same XV that opened the Nations Championship with a 28-21 victory against Japan.

Alex Mann comes in for James Botham at blind-side flanker, Aaron Wainwright is back from a leg injury at number eight, lock Ben Carter returns for the injured Adam Beard and Josh Adams gets the nod on the wing.

Botham was man of the match against New Zealand but his partner is expecting their first child this week.

Listen live on BBC Radio Wales, BBC Radio Cymru and Sports Extra on BBC Sounds

Exeter flanker Kane James is set to win his second cap from the bench after making his debut against Argentina in July.

Scarlets centre or fly-half Joe Hawkins also comes in for Ospreys playmaker Dan Edwards, who suffered an ankle injury in training that has led to Cardiff's Jarrod Evans being called into the Nations Championship squad.

Taine Plumtree will cover the second row in the absence of Beard, who suffered a shoulder injury against New Zealand.

Number eight Taine Basham and wing Gabriel Hamer-Webb drop out of the matchday squad after starting against the All Blacks.

Eleven players will have started all three Tests - eight from English clubs and the Scarlets trio of full-back Blair Murray, centre Eddie James and fly-half Sam Costelow.

Rees-Zammit: From beating All Blacks to meeting Man Utd heroes

Wales show they have bench impact in All Blacks win

After beating Japan and the All Blacks, Wales are looking to complete a Cardiff hat-trick against the Wallabies.

They then travel to Twickenham's Allianz Stadium for finals weekend when they will play a southern hemisphere opponent, which could well be another fixture against the Japanese.

Head coach Tandy said: "We were all immensely proud to make history last week.

"There's a new opportunity and challenge for us against Australia and we're looking to back up our performance this weekend.

"It's our last home game of this competition. The support that fans give to the players and staff has been incredible and we can't wait to get back out at Principality Stadium."

The Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) has stated it has already sold more than 60,000 tickets for the fixture at Principality Stadium, which holds just under 74,000.

That figure exceeds the 55,152 that witnessed history against the All Blacks, despite the late kick-off time against the Wallabies.

Exeter's Tom Hooper has been named in the second row for Australia while flanker Carlo Tizzano starts in five forward changes from the team that lost to Scotland.

The front rows rotate roles for this Test with Isaac Kailea, Brandon Paenga-Amosa and Taniela Tupou selected as the starting combination, with Angus Bell, Billy Pollard and Allan Alaalatoa the replacements.

Lock Jeremy Williams and Fraser McReight are also on the bench as Australia contend with a six-day turnaround.

Wallabies head coach Les Kiss said: "We know we need to step up against a Welsh team full of confidence and momentum after their historic win against the All Blacks last weekend.

"Pulling on the gold jersey against Wales at Principality Stadium in Cardiff creates one of the great atmospheres in world rugby and we are focused on being up for the occasion."

Wales: Murray; Rees-Zammit, E James, Llewellyn, Adams; Costelow, T Williams; Smith, Lake (capt), Griffin, Jenkins, Carter, Mann, Morgan, Wainwright.

Replacements: Elias, G Thomas, Lewis, Plumtree, K James, Morgan-Williams, Hawkins, Hennessey.

Australia: Wright; Jorgensen, Suaalii, Ikitau, Potter; Gorden, Lonergan; Kailea, Paenga-Amosa, Tupou, Canham, Hooper, Valentini, Tizzano, Wilson (capt).

Replacements: Pollard, Bell, Alaalatoa, Williams, McReight, Thomas, Donaldson, Daugunu.

Assistant referees: Karl Dickson (England) & Jeremy Rozier (France).

images.caption: Image caption, Aaron Wainwright and Josh Adams both missed the historic win over the All Blacks
